analysis.one_liner: Restores media ownership limits and the fairness doctrine to break up concentrated media ownership.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended, with 9 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rolled back media consolidation. It reinstates a rule requiring broadcasters to present conflicting views on public issues, caps any company's national TV audience reach at 35 percent, limits how many radio stations one company can own, and bars companies from owning a TV station and the overlapping local cable system. Companies already over those limits would have had one year to sell stations off.
analysis.who_benefits: Viewers, listeners, and communities that depend on local TV, radio, and newspapers. Smaller broadcasters and independent program producers would gain access to airtime now controlled by the networks. The bill's findings say two-thirds of independent newspapers have disappeared since 1975 and minority ownership of TV stations fell to 1.9 percent, so restoring ownership limits and requiring public-interest reports would give communities more say over their local news [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the 'fairness doctrine' standard in effect on January 1, 1987, requiring broadcast licensees to give reasonable opportunity for the discussion of conflicting views on issues of public importance [S3].

Caps any party's national TV audience reach at 35 percent and bars owning a TV station together with an overlapping cable system, and requires current holders above those limits to divest within one year [S3].
Limits national radio ownership to no more than 5 percent of all AM and FM stations and tightens local radio ownership caps by market size [S3].
Declares the FCC's June 2, 2003 media ownership deregulation rules invalid and reinstates the stricter rules in effect on June 1, 2003 [S3].
Limits networks from filling more than 60 percent of primetime with their own in-house programming, opening slots to independent producers [S3].
Requires every broadcast station, every two years, to report to the FCC and publish how it is serving the public interest, including local affairs programming [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large media companies. Broadcast networks and big station groups would have to sell stations to get under the 35 percent national cap; big radio chains would face new national and local ownership limits; cable operators could no longer buy the local TV stations they overlap; and all broadcasters would bear new public-interest reporting duties. Networks also could not rely on their own studios for most primetime shows [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Networks and big radio and cable companies

drawbacks.text: Restoring the 1987 fairness-doctrine rules puts government back in the position of judging whether broadcasters covered conflicting views, which critics across the political spectrum have long argued risks chilling or politicizing news judgment [S3].

The one-year forced divestiture of stations would be disruptive, and the bill itself notes that 80 percent of households have cable or satellite and 71 percent have online access, so opponents could argue audiences already have more information sources than in 1987, when the old rules fit a three-network world [S3].
Requiring networks to buy at most 60 percent of primetime from outside studios could raise costs for viewers and stations if independent production cannot match the scale of network studios [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: fewer companies controlling what communities see and hear, with forced divestiture and caps giving local stations and independent producers room. The cost is regulatory: content-coverage rules invite disputes over compliance, the ownership caps are blunt instruments that treat markets of very different sizes alike, and the divestiture deadline would cause market churn. On balance, the bill would meaningfully shift power from a handful of media conglomerates toward local and independent voices, at the price of heavier government supervision of broadcasting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications Subcommittee, which never took it up, so it died without any vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the Media Ownership Reform Act of 2004 in the House on March 30, 2004 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 8, 2004, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill ended with 9 cosponsors: 8 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with the bill never having received a committee vote or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large broadcast networks, big radio chains, and cable operators came out ahead: they kept their consolidated holdings, faced no forced divestitures, and remained under the FCC's 2003 deregulated approach rather than the stricter pre-2003 rules. Ordinary viewers and independent broadcasters gained nothing, as the ownership limits, fairness standard, and public-interest reports never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big media companies kept their stations

for.name: Rep. Maurice D. Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore media ownership limits, the fairness standard, and public-interest reporting requirements

for.name: 9 House cosponsors (8 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no additional support was recorded

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Telecommunications and the Internet Subcommittee, which never scheduled a markup or vote during the remainder of the Congress

against.name: Large broadcast, radio, and cable companies
against.role: Industry holders of the concentrated ownership the bill would unwind
against.what_they_did: No recorded action on this bill, but the bill would have forced them to divest stations and accept stricter ownership and programming rules; the committee that had jurisdiction over it never acted on it

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; sponsorship was almost entirely Democratic (8 of 9 cosponsors were Democrats, one Independent) with no Republican cosponsors listed [S4].

industries.industry: Broadcast networks and large TV station groups
industries.note: The bill caps national TV audience reach at 35 percent, bans TV-cable cross-ownership, and would force current holders above the limits to divest within a year. These companies profited from the FCC's 2003 deregulation, so their gain came at the cost of fewer independent news voices for viewers.

National ownership would be limited to 5 percent of all AM and FM stations and local caps tightened by market size, unwinding the consolidation that followed the 1996 Telecommunications Act. Concentrated radio ownership reduced local programming choices for listeners.
Operators could no longer own a TV broadcast station whose coverage overlapped their cable service area, limiting their ability to bundle control of both local programming and its distribution.

industries.industry: Independent program producers and small local broadcasters
industries.note: Caps on network-produced primetime programming (60 percent for the big four networks) would open airtime to independent studios, and tighter ownership limits preserve room for locally owned stations.
